english: Last year I traveled around Korea.
tip: 여행하다 (yeohaenghada = travel) takes a direct object: 한국을 여행했어요 (hangugeul yeohaenghaesseoyo) = 'I traveled Korea' – no 'around' or 'in' needed.

english: I took lots of photos there.
tip: 사진을 찍다 (sajineul jjikda = to take a photo) — same 찍다 as tapping a card!

english: I sent the trip photos to my family.
tip: 한테 (hante) marks a person on the receiving end: 가족한테 보냈어요 (gajokhante bonaesseoyo = sent to my family). Places take 에 (e) instead.

english: I still can't forget that trip.
tip: 못 (mot = can't) goes right before the verb: 못 잊어요 (mot ijeoyo = can't forget). It marks inability – 안 (an) would mean you simply don't.

english: Next week I'm going on a trip.
tip: 여행을 가다 (yeohaengeul gada = to go on a trip) — trips are "gone", not "made".

english: I'm going to Gangneung with a friend.
tip: 랑 (rang) is the casual spoken 'with': 친구랑 (chingurang = with a friend). In formal writing you would see 와/과 (wa/gwa) instead – same job, different register.

english: We'll book a hotel near the sea.
tip: 예약 (yeyak) reserves places; 예매 (yemae) books tickets.

english: We're going to wear hanbok.
tip: Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 (ipda) for clothes – 한복을 입을 거예요 (hanbogeul ibeul geoyeyo). Shoes take 신다 (sinda), hats 쓰다 (sseuda).

english: Where will you go on vacation?
tip: 때 (ttae = the time of): 휴가 때 (hyuga ttae = during vacation).

english: I'm going to make a travel plan.
tip: Plans are "built" in Korean: 계획을 세워요 (gyehoegeul sewoyo = make a plan).

english: I'm going to the market with a friend today.
tip: 랑 (rang) = 'with/and' after a vowel: 친구랑 (chingu-rang = with a friend).

english: I buy fruit and vegetables at the market.
tip: 이랑 (irang) = 'and/with' after a consonant: 과일이랑 야채 (gwail-irang yachae); after a vowel it's 랑 (rang).

english: On weekends the department store is crowded.
tip: English says a place is crowded; Korean says the people are many: 사람이 많아요 (saram-i manayo). The crowd is the subject, not the store.

english: The T-shirt is 15,000 won.
tip: 만 오천 (man ocheon) = 15,000 — stack 만 (10,000) + 오천 (5,000).

english: Please give me a little discount.
tip: 깎아 주세요 (kkakka juseyo) = 'please lower the price' — fine at markets, not at malls.

english: The price is a bit expensive.
tip: 좀 (jom) softens statements: 좀 비싸요 (jom bissayo = it's a bit expensive).

english: These clothes are on sale.
tip: N 중이에요 (jung-ieyo) = 'in the middle of N': 세일 중이에요 (seil jung-ieyo = it's on sale).

english: Today only, it's 5,000 won.
tip: 만 (man) after a noun = 'only': 오늘만 (oneul-man = today only) — same sound as 만 = 10,000!

english: Yesterday it was cheaper.
tip: No -er endings in Korean – comparatives just add 더 (deo = more) before the word: 더 쌌어요 (deo ssasseoyo) = was cheaper, literally 'more was-cheap'.

english: I spent too much money.
tip: 쓰다 (sseuda) = write, use, AND spend: 돈을 썼어요 (don-eul sseosseoyo = spent money).

english: I like blue.
tip: Color words end in -색 (saek): 파란색 (paransaek = blue).

english: I often wear a hat.
tip: 쓰다 also = wear on your head: 모자를 써요 (moja-reul sseoyo = I wear a hat).

english: I bought new glasses.
tip: English puts 'new' on the glasses; Korean puts it on the buying: 새로 샀어요 (saero sasseoyo = newly bought) – the adverb carries what the adjective would.

english: I'm buying a scarf as a present.
tip: 로 (ro) also marks a role: 선물로 (seonmullo = as a present) – the same particle that covers transport and direction stretches to 'in the capacity of'.

english: Try this skirt on.
tip: V-어 봐요 = 'try V-ing': 입어 봐요 (ibeo bwayo = try it on). 봐요 works as its own helper word.

english: Try the shoes on.
tip: 신다 (sinda) = wear on your FEET: 신발을 신어요 (sinbal-eul sineoyo = wear shoes).

english: What size do you wear?
tip: 몇 (myeot) asks 'what number': 몇 사이즈 (myeot saijeu = what size).

english: This size is too small for me.
tip: 한테 (hante) = 'to/for (a person)': 저한테 작아요 (jeohante jagayo = small for me).

english: The shoes are a little small.
tip: 조금 (jogeum) = a little; 좀 (jom) is its casual short form.

english: This T-shirt fits.
tip: 맞아요 (majayo) spans 'it fits' and 'that's right': 사이즈가 맞아요 (saijeu-ga majayo = the size fits) uses the same word you'd use to agree with someone.
